references.text: The hostility between Jews and Samaritans is the background for why the Samaritans did not receive Jesus. The Gospel of John confirms that Jews do not associate with Samaritans.

The Samaritan woman points to the conflict between Samaritans and Jews over the proper place of worship – Mount Gerizim versus Jerusalem. That Jesus' face was set toward Jerusalem intensified this conflict.
Jesus had decided to go to Jerusalem, which is the direct cause of the rejection in verse 53. The Samaritans would not receive someone who was heading to the rival sanctuary.
The parable of the Good Samaritan shows that Jesus nevertheless had a positive view of Samaritans, even though he was rejected by them in this instance.
A Samaritan was the only one of ten lepers who returned to thank Jesus, showing that not all Samaritans rejected him.
The disciples' reaction to the rejection – they wanted to call down fire from heaven – shows how seriously they took the rejection, but Jesus rebuked them.
The Samaritans' hostile attitude toward Jews has roots going back to the split between the northern and southern kingdoms, and their mixing with pagan peoples after the Assyrian conquest.
The Samaritans' opposition to the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem shows the deep conflict over Jerusalem as a place of worship – the same conflict that lies behind the rejection in Luke 9:53.
Despite the rejection in Samaria, the gospel was still to be preached there, as Jesus said before his ascension.
Philip preached the gospel in Samaria with great success, showing that the Samaritans' rejection of Jesus in Luke 9:53 was not final.
